newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Dutch call money falls ahead of expiry.
newsitem.headline: Dutch call money falls ahead of expiry.

text.p: Dutch call money rates dropped sharply on Thursday as participants had sufficient liquidity to meet the central bank's requirements ahead of Friday's cash reserve expiry.

Dealers said call money, falling to 2.25 percent bid earlier today, would probably move back to between 3.12 or 3.25 percent bid on Friday when the new four week cash reserve facility started running.
Overall trade was thin with only a few investors showing interest in the money market as the share market has been giving much higher returns this year.
Dealers said business was focusing on call money and short-dated deposits.
The guilder was stable in afternoon trade at 112.615 per 100 marks, although it had weakened a little earlier on during the session at 112.63 per 100 marks.

Dealers said the current exchange rate would not signal a move by the Dutch central bank, which will set a new special advances pact this afternoon at 1400 GMT. The special advances rate, currently 3.00 percent, sets the tone for money market rates.
Rabobank Nederland said the guilder-mark exchange rate remains the key for movements in Dutch interest rates, after yesterday's revision of Dutch 1996 GDP growth to 3.3 percent from 2.7 percent.

Rabobank said in its Core European Outlook it was not the domestic economy, but rather the currency market's reaction to events that might trigger a weakening of the guilder vis-a-vis the German mark.
"The red zone for the Dutch central bank would start at Mark/guilder above the central parity (1.12673 guilders)," it said.

Two weeks ago the Dutch central bank raised the special advances rate by 10 basis points to 3.00 percent as the guilder had weakened against the mark. It was trading at around 112.60 per 100 marks on the day of the rate hike.
Dealers said today they did not foresee another move by the central bank as long as the guilder stays below 112.67 per 100 marks.

Rabobank said the guilder could weaken if investors step out of guilder bonds and buy bunds or if investors take their profits and sell their Dutch shares as the Dutch market has performed better than most other European markets this year.
It said investors could start to look in other markets and this could trigger a decline in guilder demand, which could weaken the Dutch currency.
